Disney asked a dying AI firm to go bust first. That way it could hire the team and leave the lawsuits behind. So why are Disney and Google both paying for pieces of the same company? And what does it mean for you?

I've been reading the court papers on Character.AI, the app where millions of people chat with made-up characters. Two giants have now paid for pieces of it, for very different reasons. So I wanted to break it down for you.

Let's start with Google. Google wanted the brains behind the app. So in 2024, it reportedly paid two point seven billion dollars to use Character.AI's tech. And it hired the founders and their research team away. Google was racing to build the smartest AI, and these people were very good at it. But the rest of the staff stayed behind, and the app carried on, until its cash started running low.

Now, Disney wanted something else, and to see why, go back to last December. Disney agreed to put a billion dollars into OpenAI. As part of that deal, over two hundred Disney characters would star in Sora, OpenAI's video app. But Sora belonged to OpenAI. So Disney was really renting space for Mickey, Marvel and Star Wars on someone else's app.

Then in March, OpenAI shut Sora down. The deal died, and no money changed hands. Disney said it respected the decision, which is a very polite way to say, well, that's awkward.

So Disney changed its plan. In September, it hired Character.AI's chief executive, who ran the firm after the founders left. He got a brand new job, Disney's first ever technology chief. And this month, the court papers show the rest of the plan. Disney has offered jobs to sixty-six of Character.AI's staff. All together, their pay comes to about sixty million dollars a year, for three years. On top of that, Disney has bid twenty million dollars for the code. That includes its tools for keeping children safe.

Here's the clever bit. Character.AI filed for bankruptcy on the twelfth of October. And Disney made that a condition of its offer, and the papers even say why. Character.AI was running low on cash. And it faced lawsuits from families and US states, who say its chatbots harmed children. Going through the court means Disney takes the people and the code, clean, while the lawsuits stay behind with Character.AI.

So who is left holding the empty box? The people who used the app, for a start. Disney didn't bid for the app itself, or for anyone's chats. So what happens to the app is now up to the court. And then there are the people suing Character.AI, whose claims stay with a firm that is being sold for parts.

See, the money followed the people. Google paid billions for the tech and the founders, and Disney is paying millions for the rest of the team. Everyone else is left with the empty box.

And it isn't just Disney. Netflix bought an AI film start-up this year, and the record label Warner Music bought an AI firm too. The big media firms have stopped renting AI, and started owning it.

So my prediction is that three more giants follow them. First, Skydance, the new owner of Paramount Pictures. Then the record label Universal Music. And then Comcast, the American TV giant that owns NBC. By the first of March, 2027, I reckon each of them will announce buying an AI firm or its team. And I'm seventy-five percent sure all three will do it.

Now, why should you care if you're not Disney? Because most businesses now run on someone else's AI. It might be your writing tool, your chatbot, or maybe your whole customer service desk. If that supplier goes the way of Sora, the tool can switch off. And your work in it can go too. And this story shows the warning signs, years before the end.

Here's what I'd do with this info if I were you. Pick the AI tool your business leans on most, and ask four things about the firm that makes it. First, are its founders still there? Google took Character.AI's founders two years before the end. Second, is your tool the main thing that firm sells, or a side bet? Sora was a side bet, and it vanished. Third, is the firm running short of cash? The court papers warned about exactly that. And fourth, is it collecting lawsuits? That's why Disney went through the court. If two of those answers worry you, line up a plan B now. That means a second tool you've tried on real work, and a copy of your own data.
